I tried to compute this rather than recall it, and that failed — here's what happened before the knowledge-based answer.

**What I attempted (and the outcome)**

1. Searched the connected Galaxy for any ΔΔG / stability-prediction tool: `search_tools_by_name` returned **0 hits** for `stability`, `sasa`, `solvent`, `accessib`. No FoldX, Rosetta, I-Mutant, DDGun, or DSSP-type tool is installed. Structure-related tools present are only ColabFold, fpocket, Biopython align/RMSD, and PDB fetch/convert — none compute burial or folding free energy.
2. Fetched the ubiquitin crystal structure successfully: **1UBQ** (Vijay-Kumar, Bugg & Cook, 1.8 Å) uploaded from `https://files.rcsb.org/download/1UBQ.pdb` into Galaxy history `bbd44e69cb8906b50c67b6f45cd7c615`, dataset `f9cad7b01a4721352770d7b4deb3efa7`.
3. Tried to run my own Shrake–Rupley SASA + 5 Å contact-loss calculation on it as a Galaxy user-defined tool. **Blocked:** `403 err_code 403005 — "User is not allowed to run unprivileged tools"`. There is no shell available to me either, so I could not compute per-residue burial.

So the ranking below is **from my own knowledge of the ubiquitin folding literature, not from a calculation I ran.** I verified only the residue identities against the ubiquitin sequence (MQIFVKTLTGK…): position 26 = Val, 44 = Ile, 67 = Leu, so all three mutations are valid Xaa→Ala truncations of the native protein.

**Reasoning**

All three are hydrophobic-core-type residues, and all three Ala truncations are destabilising — there is no "neutral" one in this set. They differ in how much of the side chain is buried:

- **V26** sits in the most deeply buried position in ubiquitin, packed inside the α1 helix against the β-sheet, essentially fully occluded from solvent. Truncation leaves a cavity in the middle of the hydrophobic core. V26 substitutions are the classic severe destabilisers in ubiquitin folding work (V26G is used precisely because it is so destabilising).
- **L67** is largely buried in the core at the β5/helix interface; removing the isobutyl group costs substantial packing, but it is less completely occluded than V26.
- **I44** is the central residue of the **"Ile44 hydrophobic patch"** (L8–I44–H68–V70) — the recognition surface for ubiquitin-binding domains and the proteasome. Being a recognition surface, it is partially solvent-exposed, so I44A removes less buried area than the other two. Its dramatic phenotype is **loss of binding/proteasomal targeting with the fold largely intact**, not loss of stability (Beal et al., PNAS 1996).

My expectation for ΔΔG(unfolding) ordering is **V26A > L67A > I44A**, with V26A plausibly in the ~3–4 kcal/mol range, L67A ~2–3, and I44A ~1–2. I am confident in the *ordering*; I am **not** confident in those magnitudes and did not verify them — the quantitative source to check is Went & Jackson, *Protein Eng Des Sel* 18:229–237 (2005), an alanine-scan ΔΔG dataset for ubiquitin, plus Khorasanizadeh, Peters & Roder for V26 kinetics.

If you want this computed rather than recalled, the blocker is account permissions on this Galaxy (unprivileged/user-defined tools are disabled). With FoldX, Rosetta `ddg_monomer`, or even a FreeSASA run on 1UBQ I can give you actual numbers.

## ANSWER

All three destabilise ubiquitin; none is neutral.

Worst → mildest: **V26A > L67A > I44A**.

- **V26A — worst.** Most deeply buried core residue (inside α1, fully occluded); truncation leaves a core cavity.
- **L67A** — largely buried core packing at the β5/helix interface; substantial but smaller loss.
- **I44A** — least destabilising of the three (Ile44 patch is partly solvent-exposed); its major consequence is loss of ubiquitin-binding-domain/proteasome recognition, not loss of fold.

Confidence: high on the ordering, low on magnitudes. Source: my own knowledge of the ubiquitin literature (Went & Jackson 2005 alanine scan; Beal et al. PNAS 1996 for I44), **not** a computation — the available Galaxy has no ΔΔG/SASA tool and user-defined tools returned `403 err_code 403005`. 1UBQ was fetched successfully (dataset `f9cad7b01a4721352770d7b4deb3efa7`).
